correctness.rationale: The truncated body is the standard simplex in barycentric coordinates with each lambda_i<=2/3. Its vertices are exactly the permutations of (2,1,0,0)/3: two caps cannot be tight, and without a tight cap an original simplex vertex would be required. The signed determinant is affine in each point separately; at least one vertex in a convex decomposition has at least the current absolute determinant. Iterating proves a vertex-supported global maximum, not vertex-only optimality. Independent determinants in tripled barycentric coordinates with one coordinate dropped give levels 0–6 with multiplicities 78,48,192,27,120,6,24. Each determinant unit is 1/27 of the full regular tetrahedron volume, which is 72 in the given normalization. Hence the maximum is 16, and removing four disjoint 1/27-volume corners gives 16/(184/3)=6/23. Permuting the four original vertices acts transitively on the 24 maximizing four-sets. Checking fixed bases on each opposite hexagonal face gives the eight listed base–face pairs; the signed determinant is constant on the three apex vertices in each pair, hence by affinity on the full triangular face. Every maximizing vertex four-set occurs exactly once in these families.
residual_risks: No exhaustive classification of nonvertex maximizers or of other truncation depths.

value.rationale: Largest simplex volume relative to the body's volume is a natural affine-geometric benchmark on this canonical solid. The complete vertex spectrum provides the strict next-volume gap, and the eight positive-area constructions show why the existence of a vertex-supported optimum is not a rigidity statement about all optima. These precise invariants are useful for comparing candidate contained simplices and are not supplied by the general reduction alone.
residual_risks: No general capacity theorem or complete classification of continuous maximizers follows.
